entries.title: Ex-Bears kicker Robbie Gould steps down as coach at St. Viator
entries.summary: <p>Less than a week after his second season as St. Viator coach ended, Bears great Robbie Gould has resigned.</p><p>In a release, the school said Gould "made the decision to step away from coaching to spend more time with his family."</p><p>The Lions missed the IHSA playoffs in both of Gould's years in charge, going 2-7 this year and 1-8 in 2025.</p><p>"We are grateful to Coach Gould for his leadership, dedication, and commitment to our student-athletes," St. Viator president Ryan Aiello said in the statement. "We appreciate his contributions to [St.] Viator football, respect his decision to prioritize his family and wish him all the best."</p><p>Gould took over at the Arlington Heights school after one season at Rolling Meadows. The Mustangs went 5-5 and lost to St. Charles North in the first round of the Class 7A playoffs.</p><p>Before moving into high school coaching, Gould played 18 seasons in the NFL — the first 11 with the Bears from 2005-15. He set the franchise career scoring record with 1.961 points and currently ranks 10th in NFL history. After leaving the Bears, he played one season for the Giants and six for the 49ers.</p><p>St. Viator, which plays its home games off campus, has announced plans for an on-campus stadium but the project has faced pushback from neighbors.<br>The school's statement said the search for a new coach has begun.</p>

entries.title: Victims in Mundelein murder-suicide shooting identified
entries.summary: <p>Mundelein police have released the identities of five people killed in an apparent murder-suicide this week.</p><p>Five adults, all related, were found dead after a concerned family member called for a well-being check in the 200 block of Wellington Street around 11:45 p.m. Sunday, Mundelein police said.</p><p>The Lake County Coroner's Office identified the deceased as 80-Year-old James Schmidt, 77-year-old Rebecca Schmidt, 22-year-old Maclaine Schmidt, 37-year-old Nicole Heiser and 51-year-old Bryan Schmidt. </p><p>Bryan Schmidt is believed to be the alleged perpetrator, police said.</p><p>He allegedly shot his four family members before turning the gun on himself, Mundelein police said the preliminary investigation found.</p><p>Multiple suicide notes were left by Bryan Schmidt and found on the scene, police said. The shootings are believed to have taken place between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Sunday.</p><p>The family of Heiser, in a statement Wednesday, remembered the woman as a "bright, compassionate soul" who expressed deep love for animals and serving others. </p><p>"We refuse to let her be defined by this horrific violence or simply as a murder victim," the statement said. "Nicole was loyal beyond measure, generous in her time, and an esteemed animal empath — both professionally and within the community. Nicole had a great reverence for the natural world and lived with a sense of stewardship. We are so grateful for our beautiful time together and feel her presence strongly in our precious memories and calm winds."</p><p>Police said they have not had any prior contact with Bryan Schmidt and are working to determine the motive for the shooting.</p><p>Anyone with additional information on the incident is asked to call the Mundelein Police Department at 847-968-4600.</p>

entries.title: Foundry Park developers break ground on $3 billion project
entries.summary: <p>City and project officials broke ground Wednesday on Foundry Park, the $3 billion megadevelopment that promises to create a new neighborhood along the Chicago River’s North Branch — a vow that the land’s previous owner failed to keep after the pandemic.</p><p>Developer Jim Letchinger and Kayne Anderson Real Estate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/10/jdl-kayne-anderson-recalibrate-plans-lincoln-yards-parcel" >acquired</a> the northern chunk of the former Lincoln Yards development site in 2025, after previous owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/06/27/lincoln-yards-sterling-bay-jdl-development-jim-letchinger-rahm-emanuel" >Sterling Bay</a> couldn’t follow through on its ambitious plans to build towering steel and glass buildings. </p><p>Letchinger’s real estate firm, JDL Development, is breaking ground on something more scaled back: a mixed-income residential development that includes public green space and a 183-room hotel.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Scott Waguespack (32nd), JDL Development CEO Jim Letchinger, Mayor Brandon Johnson, Kayne Anderson Real Estate Chief Investment Officer David Selznick, Chicago Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright and Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) toss shovels of dirt during the groundbreaking for Foundry Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Urquhart/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The groundbreaking comes less than 10 months after JDL and Kayne Anderson notched their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/15/foundry-park-deal-gets-clearance-from-chicago-plan-commission" >first city approvals </a>from the Chicago Plan Commission in January — a speed that city officials praised at the groundbreaking on the corner of West Cortland and North Kingsbury streets.</p><p>“We took advantage of what we learned from them,” Letchinger said of Sterling Bay’s attempt at Lincoln Yards. “We go fast, and we had the capital. Capital is critical. We went through planning knowing that as soon as we get this done, we're building.”</p><p>Sterling Bay’s plans for the 53 acres of vacant land called for the equivalent of two Willis Towers’ worth of office space along the Chicago River between Bucktown and Lincoln Park — an amount that outpaced office demand after the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>The 31-acre Foundry Park is being built on the northern half of the former Lincoln Yards site and includes the old Finkl Steel property on Cortland Street, along the Chicago River.</p><p>“When I saw an opening to get involved in this incredible piece of land, I jumped at it,” Letchinger said. “Foundry Park offered a blank slate that would allow JDL to create another world-class neighborhood — and there's a lot of them in Chicago. This was an opportunity that we just could not miss.”</p><p>Plans call for more than 3,700 residences, with 20% of them affordable, and 970,000 square feet of office, retail and hotel space. Public parks, riverfront improvements and an extension of The 606 Trail are also planned.</p><p>Renderings show a mix of building heights, with the tallest at roughly 40 stories, grouped near open space and offering riverfront access. In another departure from Lincoln Yards, Foundry Park's buildings will be clad in traditional limestone and brick.</p><p>Phase one will include more than 725 residential units, retail, public green space and underground parking around Southport Avenue and Cortland and Kingsbury streets.</p><p>Letchinger is confident in the future success of Foundry Park because the mix of uses is flexible based on market demand. The homes will include rentals and for-purchase homes. Letchinger knows there’s an opportunity to build even more for-sale homes as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/01/cash-properties-sale-open-house-chicago-homebuyers-bidding-wars" >Chicago’s housing market</a> stays hot as inventory thins out.</p><p>“We know what people want,” Letchinger said. “We don't know if we can deliver all of the units right away, but we know over five, six, seven, eight years, the demand will be here. It's actually an unusual project where the more we build, the better it is because it's a neighborhood.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p>Foundry Park will benefit nearby neighborhoods like Logan Square and Lincoln Park as it takes shape, Chicago Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright said. The development will bring 8 acres of public green space, along with 2,500 jobs.</p><p>When the Cortland and Chicago River tax increment financing district expires in 2043, Foundry Park will be contributing $70 million dollars annually to citywide property taxes, according to Boatright. By 2056, the property will have contributed an estimated $1 billion, making it “one of the most consequential projects in the city's history,” she said.</p><p>The City Council’s Finance Committee approved a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/22/foundry-park-mega-project-tif-subsidy-finance-committee-approval" >$201.6 million TIF subsidy</a> for Foundry Park on Sept. 22, nearly a month before developers put shovels in the ground. Much of the funding will be used to redesign and rebuild streets, like Southport and Cortland that for decades, were closed to accommodate companies like Finkl Steel.</p><p>“Foundry Park will be a place where people will want to live, work, visit and raise families and where they can truly call themselves Chicagoans,” Boatright said.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson praised the project for its speed, jobs and mix of uses — though he joked one key element was missing.</p><p>“Looking at the renderings there, Jim, this is impressive,” Johnson said. “Everything is in this site except for our Bears stadium. I know you tried.”</p>

entries.title: 2nd woman alleging sexual assault at a University of Chicago frat house feared she was drugged: police report
entries.summary: <p>A woman told Chicago police she feared she was drugged before being sexually assaulted at a University of Chicago fraternity house earlier this year, according to a police report.</p><p>On Feb. 8, a day after the assault reportedly happened, the 19-year-old told officers the alleged assailant gave her a shot of alcohol that “might have been laced,” the report says.</p><p>“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” the woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/jane-doe-comes-forward-about-reported-rape-at-university-of-chicago-fraternity-ahead-of-public-safety-meeting/4005795/" target="_blank" >told NBC News</a>. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >The woman filed a lawsuit</a> Monday against the local and national Alpha Delta Phi organizations, alleging a member of the fraternity had assaulted “her limp body” during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi house, 5747 S. University Ave. The woman was identified only as “Jane Doe.”</p><p>The lawsuit came soon after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >another woman reported she was sexually assaulted</a> on Oct. 11 at an off-campus party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house, located just a block away at 5625 S. University Ave. Witnesses in that case reported the accuser appeared “significantly more intoxicated than expected based on her reported alcohol consumption," according to another police report.</p><p>The two cases have placed the University of Chicago at the center of a national reckoning over sexual violence at colleges, sparked by reports of gang rape and drugging at a fraternity house at Cornell University in upstate New York. </p><p>The school's Public Safety Advisory Council, comprised of students, faculty, staff, and community members, discussed sexual misconduct on campus at a Wednesday night meeting. The council couldn't answer questions about the specific reported sexual assaults, but said it could make an official recommendation to the administration on how to address sexual assault on and near campus.</p><p>"This is literally the first time we've touched on this topic," said Sharon Fairley, a professor at the university's law school and chair of the council. "This is a learning process for us ... we're in the very early stages right now to see if this is a topic that is of such interest to the community where we feel like there may be a policy gap and we do want to make a recommendation, so we haven't gotten there yet."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The building hosts the university’s Public Safety Advisory Council meetings.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The University of Chicago previously alerted students to <a class="Link" href="https://safety-security.uchicago.edu/News-Alerts/2022-11-03-Security-and-Safety-Notice" target="_blank" >a spate of alleged druggings</a> in November 2022, warning of seven reports of undergraduates who suspected their drinks had been spiked at parties.</p><p>In one case, a student reported they were “likely sexually assaulted.” The university said at the time that “such behavior is unacceptable, not tolerated within this community, and may be criminal.”</p><p>Elizabeth Spratt, former toxicology director for Westchester County in New York, said “timing is everything” when it comes to testing for potential drugs, noting levels could be low by the following morning. "These [cases] break my heart, because they're ... hard to prove because of timing," Spratt said.</p><p>The women alleging they were assaulted at the two fraternity houses aren’t students at the University of Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-dd0000" name="html-embed-module-dd0000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BBkuP"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BBkuP/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The woman identified in her lawsuit as Jane Doe said she had two shots of alcohol at the Alpha Delta Phi house before meeting the alleged assailant, according to the police report. The suspect, identified in the lawsuit and the report as Kevin Shim, then gave Jane Doe another shot, after which she told police she “vaguely remembers anything,” the report says.</p><p>“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” the woman told NBC News. “I’ve never felt like that before.”</p><p>In the lawsuit, she said she felt “unsteady and lightheaded” almost immediately after taking the drink. She was then brought to an upstairs bedroom where the fraternity member assaulted her and left her “alone and unconscious,” according to the lawsuit.</p><p>“I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC.</p><p>Other fraternity members blocked her friends from getting to the bedroom as the assault was happening, the lawsuit says.</p><p>Jane Doe went to Chicago police the next morning and was treated at Illinois Masonic Hospital, according to the lawsuit and the report.</p><p>The lawsuit doesn’t mention she was potentially drugged, but her lawyer continued to raise that allegation in an interview.</p><p>“This situation is someone that really took all the right steps,” Georgia Booth, one of Jane Doe’s attorneys, said in an interview. “The next morning, she went to the hospital, got a toxicology report and a rape kit done, and then immediately spoke to the Chicago Police Department.”</p><p>Alcohol-involved sexual assault is incredibly common on college campuses, according to Erin O'Callaghan, an assistant professor at Colorado State University. In some cases, it is combined with drug use, either voluntarily or involuntarily, said O'Callaghan, who researches substance-involved sexual violence.</p><p>While voluntary substance use is still more common, there is limited national research on drink "spiking," particularly as the types of drugs used continue to evolve, according to O'Callaghan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Booth said she’s requested additional information but has only been provided the original incident report — and not the findings of the toxicology or sexual assault testing.</p><p>Booth said she had “no idea” why there still weren’t any charges in the case.</p><p>“Unfortunately, I work with survivors of sexual assaults primarily in my practice,” Booth said. “I work with clients that have made similar reports to the Chicago Police Department. Sometimes they get little to no investigation done into their experience. So we're encouraging the police department to continue investigating, and hopefully charges will be brought soon.”</p><p>The university, the police department and the national Alpha Delta Phi organization didn’t respond to questions Wednesday.</p><p>The university previously said the allegations in the lawsuit were “disturbing.”</p><p>“The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault,” the spokesperson said in a statement Tuesday. “The University is not a defendant in the lawsuit against the fraternity. The University will cooperate by providing information and is prepared to help the Chicago Police Department in its investigation.”</p><p>At Wednesday's meeting, which drew a packed crowd inside the Drexel Building, Belinda Cortez Vasquez, associate dean of students for Student Affairs, listed university resources, including the University of Chicago Sexual Assault Dean-on-Call Program and the school's Center of Awareness, Resolution, Education and Support. </p><p>Students and staff are required to complete a training program on sexual misconduct, which Fairley said is "very, very comprehensive," but the council couldn't answer a question about following up on the training and tracking its effectiveness.</p><p>Kyle Bowman, chief of the University of Chicago Police Department, acknowledged that the climate surrounding sexual assault at the university has become increasingly tense in the wake of the two reports.</p><p>"I'm just gonna be blunt, the first thing we need to do is tell men not to commit sexual assault, to respect the people that they're with," Bowman said.</p><p>When asked if members of fraternities or sororities should be subject to specific training, Bowman didn't directly answer, but said the police department starts each quarter with safety presentations in residence halls and social spaces on campus.</p><p>Alpha Delta Phi said "the member involved" was suspended from the fraternity after the organization became aware of the reported assault, which it takes “extremely seriously.” Shim hasn't responded to a request for comment.</p><div entries.title: DuPage County confirms measles case for vaccinated resident who traveled through O'Hare Airport
entries.summary: <p>A DuPage County resident with a confirmed case of measles traveled through O’Hare International Airport last week, health officials announced Wednesday.</p><p>The resident was vaccinated and returned from an international trip last Thursday, according to the DuPage County Health Department.</p><p>Health officials said it was “uncommon” for a vaccinated person to test positive for measles, but it was possible “when there is intense or prolonged exposure to a person with measles.”</p><p>“Our community’s safety is our priority,” said Adam Forker, executive director of the DCHD. “Our team is actively working on following up with individuals who may have been potentially exposed. Vaccination continues to provide strong protection, even in a rare breakthrough case.”</p><p>Health officials said they were working to contact anyone who may have been exposed.</p><p>Anyone who was at O'Hare Airport, Terminal 5 on Oct. 15 between 4:20 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. should contact DCHD at 630-682-7400.</p><p>As of Wednesday, there were 24 confirmed cases of measles so far this year, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/10/2nd-measles-case-confirmed-in-kane-county" target="_blank" ><u>Last month</u></a>, health officials confirmed an out-of-state traveler with measles traveled through Union Station.</p><p>The stricken traveler was at Union Station on Aug. 27 after 8 p.m. through Aug. 28, according to a statement from the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p>

entries.title: Bulls add much-needed size with veteran Zach Collins finally returning
entries.summary: <p>It was an important night for Bulls veteran Zach Collins on Wednesday.</p><p>Simply because he played.</p><p>No small feat for the 6-foot-9 big, who had last played in an NBA game back on Dec. 27, 2025, before eventually undergoing season-ending surgery on his right toe. Just one of the injury issues that plagued Collins last year.</p><p>After a stellar start to his 2025 preseason, Collins fractured his left wrist and was lost until the start of December. He returned and was used as a double big in the Bulls’ lineup, doing so with some solid results. All Collins did in his 10 games was help the Bulls to a 6-4 record, averaging 9.7 points and 5.6 rebounds per game, but more importantly adding a physicality piece that the roster sorely lacked.</p><p>That’s why the new regime signed him to a two-year, $17-million deal on the first day of free agency, knowing he had injury issues.</p><p>He was slowed this preseason with a quad injury but finally came off the bench and got some run against Toronto. Call it easing Collins back into it with coach Tiago Splitter admitting the veteran was on a minutes restriction of 12-to-16 minutes for the time being.</p><p>“The tough part about Zach is he didn’t play yet,” Splitter said. “He didn’t play much last year, so we slowly want to put him there in the rotation and see those combinations, playing double-big or not. We’re going to have time to see it, have a small sample there, but we will try different combinations.”</p><p></p><p><b>King for a day</b></p><p></p><p>To further honor former Bulls broadcaster Stacey King in Wednesday’s opener, his broadcast partner Adam Amin wanted to call the first quarter by himself, leaving King’s chair empty. Robbie Hummel then joined the broadcast in the second quarter.</p><p>King died back in June after spending nearly 20 years as the color analyst for the Bulls.</p><p>The team also debuted their King patch that they will wear on their jerseys all season.</p><p></p><p><b>Rookie privilege?</b></p><p></p><p>Most NBA teams work the same when handling pregame shooting order during warmups. The veterans go last, while the rookies and deep bench guys get their work in early.</p><p>So it was a bit strange in the preseason that the Bulls’ Caleb Wilson was not only in the final group, but at home games even gets his own music played, usually the lyrics of Chicago rapper Lucki.</p><p>If this was some No. 4 overall pick flexing his muscle to get special treatment, however, Wilson put that to rest.</p><p>“Honestly, I don’t know how that happened, being in the last (pregame shooting) slot,” Wilson said. “I just told them give me whatever was available and then the (United Center) DJ, he’s cool, got the mohawk. I met him when we did media day and he knew my favorite artist was Lucki, so every time I come out, he plays him for me.”</p><p>And just to make sure Wilson was reminded he is still a rookie? Veteran Norman Powell made all the young guys use pink “Hello Kitty” luggage for the trip to Toronto.</p><p></p><p><b>Staying put</b></p><p></p><p>The traveling party was a bit thinner for this two-game road trip with rookie Dailyn Swain and guard Jordan Hawkins staying back in Chicago to deal with illness.</p><p>The Bulls play the Bucks on Friday so both players could possibly join the team in Milwaukee, but Splitter wasn’t going to force the issue, especially since Swain and Hawkins were on the outside looking in as far as the rotation.</p>

entries.title: Bulls get thumped in season debut as rebuild looks like demolition site
entries.summary: <p>A Norman Powell missed floater, a Josh Giddey errant pass, and then a welcome-to-the-Association moment when rookie Caleb Wilson was stripped by a player he idolized growing up in Kawhi Leonard.</p><p>All just 90 seconds into Wednesday’s Bulls season opener, transforming a perceived rebuild into something that resembled more like a demolition site.</p><p>And just like that Bulls basketball debuted to a resounding thud.</p><p>Was the 135-92 trouncing – the worst loss in a season opener in Bulls history – unexpected? Not really. But with all the excitement around the team – whether it was the high-flying No. 4 pick in Wilson, new coach Tiago Splitter or just the gloomy clouds that seemed to leave with the arrival of the new front office, it was supposed to feel a lot better than it looked.</p><p>A reminder of the reality of the NBA: Good feelings only last so long because at some point the game has to be played.</p><p>Maybe that’s why Splitter called a timeout just 90 seconds into the game, as he saw his young team down 7-0 and drowning.</p><p>A life preserver that only kept his team afloat for so long.</p><p>“The way we competed,” Splitter said of what bothered him most about that start. “After a turnover, getting our heads down when running back, that’s something we cannot accept. Talked to them at halftime, after the game, we gotta be better.”</p><p>It seemingly can’t get worse.</p><p>Through most of the game, the deficit was in the 30ss, even reaching as much as 48 points. An Eastern Conference contender against a team that will be fighting to stay out of the bottom three of the league all season long on full display.</p><p>Also on display?</p><p>An All-Star frontcourt in Leonard and Scottie Barnes against two youngsters in Wilson and Matas Buzelis. Men dealing with boys.</p><p>No wonder Splitter was concerned with the matchup. Not just in the frontcourt but the entire roster, especially on the defensive end where there weren’t a lot of answers.</p><p>“We knew they had guys that can steal the ball, and we knew a lot about their physicality,” Splitter said. “Sometimes you gotta feel it and know it when you go there and play.”</p><p>Wilson did just that, finishing with 16 points, but doing so on a 7-of-21 shooting night with nine turnovers and a minus-45 in plus/minus.</p><p>“Obviously it was a bad night for Caleb,” Splitter said. “We’re going to grow from this, learn from this. He was playing too much in crowds, not passing the ball when he had two, three guys on him, so we’re going to watch film and get better.”</p><p>Considering the Bulls (0-1) finished 27-of-85 (32%) from the field and 4-of-36 (11%) from three, while allowing the Raptors to shoot 44-of-98 (45%) and turn them over 27 times, getting better should be a low bar.</p><p>Wilson agreed with Splitter that he had to experience an NBA game as the ultimate teacher.</p><p>“I just got to figure it out,” Wilson said. “That’s the great thing about the NBA is we play 82 games, so able to watch film, my coaches tell me things I can do better, so it’s about going out there and doing it. Flim is a great way to see where you should be and could be, but you just got to go out there and do it.”</p><p>They’ll have a practice in Toronto on Thursday to do just that before taking on Milwaukee in an afternoon tilt on Friday.</p><p>“Yes, I’m worried about that,” Splitter responded when asked about making sure his team doesn’t fall into bad habits. “We got to get better.”</p>
